_link.title: I can distinguish between the movement of substances in hypertonic, isotonic and hypotonic environments for animal cells

toLevel2.stem: What happens to an animal cell placed in a hypertonic solution?

options.text: It shrinks as water moves out
options.explanation: In a hypertonic solution, the external solute concentration is higher, so water leaves the cell by osmosis and the cell shrinks.

options.text: It swells as water moves in
options.explanation: Swelling occurs in a hypotonic solution, not a hypertonic one.

options.text: It stays the same exact size
options.explanation: The cell stays the same size in an isotonic solution, not a hypertonic one.

options.text: It divides into two new cells
options.explanation: Cell division is not caused by changes in tonicity.

toLevel2.stem: What is the term for the bursting of a red blood cell in a hypotonic solution?

options.text: Haemolysis
options.explanation: Haemolysis is the bursting of a red blood cell when water enters by osmosis in a hypotonic solution.

options.text: Crenation
options.explanation: Crenation is the shrinking of an animal cell in a hypertonic solution.

options.text: Plasmolysis
options.explanation: Plasmolysis occurs in plant cells, not animal cells.

options.text: Osmolysis
options.explanation: Osmolysis is not a standard biological term; the correct term is haemolysis.

toLevel2.stem: What is the term for the shrinking of an animal cell in a hypertonic solution?

options.text: Crenation
options.explanation: Crenation describes the shrinking and wrinkling of an animal cell as water leaves by osmosis.

options.text: Haemolysis
options.explanation: Haemolysis is the bursting of red blood cells, not their shrinking.

options.text: Turgidity
options.explanation: Turgidity describes swollen plant cells, not shrunken animal cells.

options.text: Plasmolysis
options.explanation: Plasmolysis refers to the shrinking of plant cell contents away from the cell wall.

toLevel2.stem: In an isotonic solution, what happens to an animal cell?

options.text: It maintains its normal shape
options.explanation: In an isotonic solution the solute concentration is equal on both sides, so there is no net water movement and the cell keeps its shape.

options.text: It bursts due to water entry
options.explanation: Bursting occurs in a hypotonic solution, not an isotonic one.

options.text: It shrinks due to water leaving
options.explanation: Shrinking occurs in a hypertonic solution, not an isotonic one.

options.text: It doubles in size very rapidly
options.explanation: An isotonic solution does not cause any change in cell volume.

toLevel2.stem: Why does an animal cell burst in a hypotonic solution?

options.text: Water enters by osmosis and the cell has no cell wall to resist swelling
options.explanation: Animal cells lack a cell wall, so when water enters by osmosis the membrane stretches until the cell bursts.

options.text: Solutes rush into the cell and cause it to explode from chemical reactions
options.explanation: Bursting is caused by water entering, not by solutes rushing in.

options.text: The cell membrane dissolves when exposed to any hypotonic solution in water
options.explanation: The membrane does not dissolve; it ruptures from excessive internal pressure.

options.text: The nucleus expands and pushes the membrane open from the inside of the cell
options.explanation: The entire cell swells due to water entry, not just the nucleus.

toLevel2.stem: An animal cell placed in a hypertonic solution will undergo crenation as water leaves the cell.

options.text: True
options.explanation: In a hypertonic solution water moves out of the animal cell, causing it to shrink and crenate.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is correct; crenation occurs when water leaves an animal cell in a hypertonic solution.

toLevel2.stem: Animal cells remain at their normal size in a hypotonic solution.

options.text: True
options.explanation: In a hypotonic solution water enters the cell, causing it to swell and potentially burst.

options.text: False
options.explanation: Animal cells swell in a hypotonic solution because water enters by osmosis.

toLevel2.stem: A red blood cell placed in distilled water will {{blank:1}} because distilled water is {{blank:2}} to the cell.

options.text: swell and burst
options.explanation: Water enters the cell by osmosis, causing it to swell until it bursts (haemolysis).

options.text: shrink and wrinkle
options.explanation: Shrinking occurs in a hypertonic solution, not in distilled water.

options.text: stay the same size
options.explanation: The cell would stay the same in an isotonic solution, not in distilled water.

options.text: hypotonic
options.explanation: Distilled water has no solutes, making it hypotonic relative to the cell.

options.text: hypertonic
options.explanation: Distilled water has fewer solutes than the cell; it is hypotonic, not hypertonic.

options.text: isotonic
options.explanation: Distilled water has no solutes, so it is not isotonic to any living cell.

toLevel2.stem: In a hypertonic solution, water moves {{blank:1}} of the animal cell, causing {{blank:2}}.

options.text: out
options.explanation: Water moves from the area of higher free water concentration (inside) to lower (outside).

options.text: into
options.explanation: Water moves into the cell in a hypotonic solution, not a hypertonic one.

options.text: around
options.explanation: Water moves across the membrane during osmosis, not around the cell.

options.text: crenation
options.explanation: Crenation is the shrinking of an animal cell as it loses water.

options.text: haemolysis
options.explanation: Haemolysis is the bursting of cells, which occurs in hypotonic solutions.

options.text: turgidity
options.explanation: Turgidity describes swollen plant cells; animal cells crenate in hypertonic solutions.

toLevel2.stem: An animal cell maintains its normal shape in an {{blank:1}} solution because there is no {{blank:2}} movement of water.

options.text: isotonic
options.explanation: An isotonic solution has equal solute concentration inside and outside the cell.

options.text: hypotonic
options.explanation: A hypotonic solution would cause water to enter and the cell to swell.

options.text: hypertonic
options.explanation: A hypertonic solution would cause water to leave and the cell to shrink.

options.text: net
options.explanation: Water moves in both directions equally, resulting in no net change in volume.

options.text: any
options.explanation: Water molecules still move across the membrane, but there is no net movement.

options.text: rapid
options.explanation: The key point is no net movement, not the speed of movement.

toLevel3.stem: Why do animal cells lyse in a hypotonic solution but plant cells do not?

options.text: Animal cells lack a cell wall to resist the internal water pressure
options.explanation: Without a rigid cell wall, the animal cell membrane cannot withstand the pressure from incoming water and ruptures.

options.text: Plant cells have more water inside so osmosis does not occur in them
options.explanation: Osmosis occurs in both cell types; the difference is the presence of a cell wall in plant cells.

options.text: Animal cells absorb water faster because their membranes are more permeable
options.explanation: The rate of water entry is not the key factor; the lack of a cell wall causes lysis in animal cells.

options.text: Plant cells are immune to osmosis because their vacuole blocks all water entry
options.explanation: Plant cells are not immune to osmosis; the cell wall prevents bursting, not the vacuole.

toLevel3.stem: A student places red blood cells in 0.9% saline and observes no change. What does this tell us about the saline solution?

options.text: It is isotonic to the red blood cells
options.explanation: No change in cell shape indicates equal solute concentration on both sides, confirming isotonicity.

options.text: It is hypotonic to the red blood cells
options.explanation: A hypotonic solution would cause the cells to swell, not remain unchanged.

options.text: It is hypertonic to the red blood cells
options.explanation: A hypertonic solution would cause the cells to shrink, not remain unchanged.

options.text: It has blocked osmosis from occurring across the cell membrane entirely
options.explanation: Osmosis still occurs; water moves in both directions equally, producing no net change.

toLevel3.stem: Why is crenation different from plasmolysis even though both involve water loss?

options.text: In crenation the whole cell shrinks, while in plasmolysis only the membrane pulls from the wall
options.explanation: Animal cells shrink entirely (crenation) because they lack a cell wall; plant cells retain their wall shape while the membrane detaches (plasmolysis).

options.text: Crenation involves water entering the cell while plasmolysis involves water leaving it
options.explanation: Both processes involve water leaving the cell; the difference is the structural response.

options.text: Plasmolysis occurs in animal cells while crenation occurs exclusively in plant cells
options.explanation: This is reversed; crenation occurs in animal cells and plasmolysis in plant cells.

options.text: There is no difference between the two processes as they are exactly the same thing
options.explanation: They differ because of the presence or absence of a cell wall.

toLevel3.stem: Why must hospital IV drips use isotonic saline rather than pure water?

options.text: Pure water is hypotonic and would cause red blood cells to swell and burst
options.explanation: Pure water has no solutes, creating a hypotonic environment that drives water into cells, causing haemolysis.

options.text: Pure water is hypertonic and would cause red blood cells to shrink immediately
options.explanation: Pure water is hypotonic, not hypertonic; it would cause swelling, not shrinking.

options.text: Saline contains vitamins that pure water lacks for proper cell nutrition
options.explanation: The reason is osmotic balance, not nutritional content.

options.text: Pure water is toxic to all human cells regardless of the concentration used
options.explanation: Pure water is not inherently toxic; the issue is the osmotic imbalance it creates.

toLevel3.stem: How does osmosis explain the swelling of an animal cell in a hypotonic solution?

options.text: Water moves from the higher free water concentration outside to lower inside the cell
options.explanation: In a hypotonic solution, there is more free water outside the cell, so water diffuses in by osmosis.

options.text: Solutes are actively pumped into the cell, pulling water molecules along with them
options.explanation: Swelling is caused by passive osmosis, not active solute pumping.

options.text: The cell membrane actively expands by incorporating new phospholipids from the solution
options.explanation: The membrane stretches from water entry, not from incorporating new lipids.

options.text: The hypotonic solution physically pushes against the membrane forcing it to expand
options.explanation: Swelling results from osmotic water entry, not from external physical pressure.

toLevel3.stem: What would happen if a red blood cell were transferred from an isotonic to a hypertonic solution?

options.text: Water would leave the cell and it would crenate
options.explanation: The higher external solute concentration draws water out by osmosis, causing the cell to shrink and crenate.

options.text: Water would enter the cell and it would undergo haemolysis immediately
options.explanation: Haemolysis occurs in hypotonic solutions when water enters; moving to hypertonic causes water loss.

options.text: The cell would remain unchanged because it was already at equilibrium before
options.explanation: Moving to a hypertonic solution changes the concentration gradient, causing water loss.

options.text: The cell would divide because the concentration change stimulates cell division
options.explanation: Tonicity changes do not trigger cell division; they affect cell volume through osmosis.

toLevel3.stem: Animal cells cannot survive in pure water for long because the hypotonic environment causes them to swell and lyse.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Pure water is hypotonic; water enters by osmosis, and without a cell wall, animal cells burst.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This is correct; animal cells lack a cell wall and will lyse in pure water.

toLevel3.stem: Animal cells burst in hypotonic solutions because they lack a {{blank:1}} to resist the {{blank:2}} caused by water entry.

options.text: cell wall
options.explanation: The cell wall in plant cells provides resistance; animal cells lack this structure.

options.text: nucleus
options.explanation: The nucleus contains DNA; it does not provide structural resistance to swelling.

options.text: vacuole
options.explanation: Vacuoles store materials but do not prevent cell bursting.

options.text: swelling
options.explanation: Water entering by osmosis causes the cell to swell until the membrane ruptures.

options.text: shrinking
options.explanation: Shrinking occurs in hypertonic solutions; water entry causes swelling.

options.text: dividing
options.explanation: Cell division is not caused by osmotic pressure; swelling is.

toLevel3.stem: Hospital IV drips use {{blank:1}} saline because it is isotonic, preventing red blood cells from undergoing {{blank:2}}.

options.explanation: 0.9% NaCl matches the solute concentration of blood plasma, making it isotonic.
10% saline would be hypertonic and cause crenation of blood cells.
0.01% saline would be hypotonic and could cause haemolysis.

options.text: haemolysis
options.explanation: Isotonic saline prevents the osmotic entry of water that would cause red blood cells to burst.

options.text: mitosis
options.explanation: Mitosis is cell division; it is not prevented by isotonic saline.

options.text: photosynthesis
options.explanation: Red blood cells do not perform photosynthesis.

toLevel3.stem: Crenation differs from plasmolysis because animal cells shrink {{blank:1}} while plant cells retain their {{blank:2}} shape.

options.text: entirely
options.explanation: Without a cell wall, the entire animal cell shrinks and wrinkles during crenation.

options.text: partially
options.explanation: Animal cells shrink as a whole because they lack a rigid cell wall.

options.text: temporarily
options.explanation: The extent is not about timing; it is about the whole cell shrinking versus the membrane detaching.

options.text: outer wall
options.explanation: The rigid cell wall maintains the plant cell's outer shape during plasmolysis.

options.text: membrane
options.explanation: The membrane pulls away from the wall during plasmolysis; it does not maintain shape.

options.text: vacuole
options.explanation: The vacuole shrinks during plasmolysis; it is the cell wall that maintains shape.

toLevel4.stem: A student accidentally uses 5% NaCl instead of 0.9% NaCl for a blood smear preparation. What would the red blood cells look like under the microscope?

options.text: Shrunken and wrinkled due to crenation from the hypertonic solution
options.explanation: 5% NaCl is strongly hypertonic, causing water to leave the red blood cells rapidly, resulting in crenation.

options.text: Swollen and round due to haemolysis from the hypertonic solution used
options.explanation: 5% NaCl is hypertonic, not hypotonic; cells would shrink, not swell.

options.text: Normal in shape because NaCl concentration does not affect red blood cells
options.explanation: NaCl concentration directly affects cell volume through osmosis.

options.text: Completely transparent because the salt dissolved the cell membrane fully
options.explanation: Salt does not dissolve membranes; the cells would shrink due to osmotic water loss.

toLevel4.stem: A patient with severe dehydration needs fluid replacement. Why would a hypotonic IV solution be dangerous?

options.text: It could cause red blood cells to swell and burst due to excess water entry
options.explanation: A hypotonic IV solution would create an osmotic gradient driving water into blood cells, potentially causing haemolysis.

options.text: It would cause red blood cells to shrink, reducing oxygen-carrying capacity greatly
options.explanation: Shrinking would occur with a hypertonic solution; a hypotonic one causes swelling.

options.text: It would have no effect on blood cells because dehydrated cells resist osmosis
options.explanation: Dehydrated cells still respond to osmosis; a hypotonic solution would cause water entry.

options.text: It would thicken the blood plasma, making it difficult to circulate through vessels
options.explanation: A hypotonic solution dilutes plasma; it does not thicken it.

toLevel4.stem: A forensic scientist finds blood stains at a crime scene washed with tap water. Many red blood cells appear as empty membranes ('ghost cells'). What happened?

options.text: Tap water is hypotonic, causing haemolysis and leaving behind empty membranes
options.explanation: Tap water is hypotonic to red blood cells; water entered by osmosis, the cells burst, and the contents leaked out leaving ghost cells.

options.text: Tap water is hypertonic, causing the cells to shrink and lose their contents
options.explanation: Tap water is hypotonic; hypertonic solutions cause crenation, not the formation of ghost cells.

options.text: The tap water dissolved the entire cell including the membrane leaving nothing
options.explanation: The membrane remains intact as a 'ghost'; the contents leaked out after haemolysis.

options.text: Ghost cells form when blood dries out naturally regardless of any water exposure
options.explanation: Ghost cells specifically result from haemolysis caused by exposure to a hypotonic environment.

toLevel4.stem: A student places red blood cells in three solutions and records: Solution A — cells burst; Solution B — no change; Solution C — cells shrink. Which is hypertonic?

options.text: Solution C
options.explanation: Cell shrinking indicates a hypertonic solution where water leaves the cells by osmosis.

options.text: Solution A
options.explanation: Cell bursting indicates a hypotonic solution, not a hypertonic one.

options.text: Solution B
options.explanation: No change indicates an isotonic solution.

options.text: All three solutions
options.explanation: Only Solution C is hypertonic; the others are hypotonic (A) and isotonic (B).

toLevel4.stem: Contact lens solution must be isotonic to the fluid in the eye. What would happen if a person used a hypertonic solution on their eyes?

options.text: Water would leave the eye cells, causing irritation and discomfort from cell shrinkage
options.explanation: A hypertonic solution draws water out of the eye cells by osmosis, causing crenation and irritation.

options.text: The eye cells would swell and burst from excessive water entry caused by osmosis
options.explanation: Swelling and bursting would occur with a hypotonic solution, not a hypertonic one.

options.text: Nothing would happen because eye cells are resistant to all osmotic changes naturally
options.explanation: Eye cells are affected by osmosis like all animal cells.

options.text: The contact lenses would dissolve because the hypertonic solution is too concentrated
options.explanation: Contact lenses are made of synthetic materials not affected by tonicity; the issue is cell damage.

toLevel4.stem: A kidney dialysis machine filters waste from blood using a solution. Why must this solution be isotonic to blood plasma?

options.text: To prevent red blood cells from crenating or lysing during the dialysis process
options.explanation: An isotonic solution ensures no net water movement, keeping blood cells at their normal volume during treatment.

options.text: To ensure maximum waste removal by creating a strong osmotic gradient across cells
options.explanation: A strong osmotic gradient would damage cells; isotonic conditions protect them while waste is filtered.

options.text: To provide nutrients to the blood that are missing due to the kidney failure
options.explanation: The primary purpose is osmotic balance, not nutrition.

options.text: To sterilise the blood by killing any bacteria present in the bloodstream naturally
options.explanation: Dialysis removes waste; sterilisation is not its purpose and tonicity does not kill bacteria.

toLevel4.stem: A scientist wants to isolate the contents of red blood cells for analysis. Which solution should they place the cells in?

options.text: A hypotonic solution to cause haemolysis and release the cell contents
options.explanation: A hypotonic solution causes water to enter, bursting the cells and releasing their contents for analysis.

options.text: A hypertonic solution to shrink the cells and squeeze the contents out
options.explanation: Hypertonic solutions cause crenation, which traps contents inside the shrunken cell.

options.text: An isotonic solution to keep cells stable while extracting contents through the membrane
options.explanation: An isotonic solution keeps cells intact; it does not release their contents.

options.text: A concentrated acid to dissolve the cells and release everything at once immediately
options.explanation: Acid would denature proteins and destroy the contents; a hypotonic solution is gentler and preserves them.

toLevel4.stem: If 5% NaCl were used instead of 0.9% NaCl for a blood preparation, red blood cells would undergo {{blank:1}} because the solution is {{blank:2}}.

options.text: crenation
options.explanation: 5% NaCl is strongly hypertonic, causing water to leave the cells and the cells to shrink.

options.text: haemolysis
options.explanation: Haemolysis occurs in hypotonic solutions; 5% NaCl is hypertonic.

options.text: mitosis
options.explanation: Mitosis is cell division, unrelated to tonicity effects.

options.text: hypertonic
options.explanation: 5% NaCl has a much higher solute concentration than blood cells.

options.text: hypotonic
options.explanation: 5% NaCl is hypertonic, not hypotonic.

options.text: isotonic
options.explanation: 0.9% NaCl is isotonic; 5% is hypertonic.

toLevel4.stem: Ghost cells are formed when red blood cells undergo {{blank:1}} in a hypotonic solution, leaving behind the {{blank:2}}.

options.text: haemolysis
options.explanation: Haemolysis causes the cell contents to leak out, leaving the membrane as a ghost cell.

options.text: crenation
options.explanation: Crenation causes shrinking, not the emptying of cell contents.

options.text: plasmolysis
options.explanation: Plasmolysis is a plant cell process involving the membrane pulling from the wall.

options.text: empty membrane
options.explanation: After haemolysis the membrane remains intact but the contents have been released.

options.text: intact nucleus
options.explanation: Mature red blood cells lack a nucleus; the remaining structure is the membrane.

options.text: cell wall shell
options.explanation: Animal cells do not have a cell wall; the ghost cell is the remaining membrane.

toLevel4.stem: To isolate the contents of red blood cells, a scientist would place them in a {{blank:1}} solution to cause the cells to {{blank:2}}.

options.text: hypotonic
options.explanation: A hypotonic solution causes water to enter the cells, eventually bursting them and releasing contents.

options.text: hypertonic
options.explanation: A hypertonic solution would shrink the cells, not burst them.

options.text: isotonic
options.explanation: An isotonic solution would keep the cells intact, not release their contents.

options.text: burst
options.explanation: The cells burst (haemolysis) releasing their contents for analysis.

options.text: shrink
options.explanation: Shrinking traps contents inside; bursting releases them.

options.text: divide
options.explanation: Cell division does not release cell contents for analysis.

toLevel5.stem: A graph shows the percentage of intact red blood cells at different NaCl concentrations. Between 0.4% and 0.2% NaCl, the percentage drops sharply from 100% to 0%. What does this suggest?

options.text: Individual red blood cells have slightly different internal solute concentrations
options.explanation: The gradual drop across a range of concentrations indicates variation in internal solute concentration among cells, with different cells lysing at different points.

options.text: All red blood cells have identical internal solute concentrations precisely at 0.3%
options.explanation: If all cells were identical, the drop would be sudden at one point, not gradual across a range.

options.text: Red blood cells are resistant to osmosis between 0.4% and 0.2% NaCl concentrations
options.explanation: The cells are not resistant; they are lysing progressively across this range.

options.text: The NaCl concentration has no effect on red blood cells below 0.4% in any situation
options.explanation: The data clearly shows progressive cell lysis below 0.4% NaCl.

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that since animal cells can't survive in pure water, they are less adaptable than plant cells. Evaluate this claim.

options.text: Oversimplified; animal cells have other adaptations like osmoregulatory organs for water balance
options.explanation: While individual animal cells lyse in pure water, multicellular animals have kidneys and other organs that maintain internal osmotic balance.

options.text: Completely correct; plant cells are superior to animal cells in every environment possible
options.explanation: Plant and animal cells have different adaptations suited to their respective environments.

options.text: Completely incorrect; animal cells are actually more adaptable because they can change shape
options.explanation: Shape change does not make animal cells more adaptable to osmotic stress than plant cells.

options.text: Correct; animal cells should evolve a cell wall to survive in all aquatic environments
options.explanation: Animal cells have alternative strategies for osmotic regulation; evolving a cell wall is not necessary.

toLevel5.stem: Freshwater amoebae have contractile vacuoles that pump out excess water. What does this reveal about their internal environment relative to freshwater?

options.text: Their internal environment is hypertonic relative to freshwater, so water constantly enters
options.explanation: The amoeba's cytoplasm has a higher solute concentration than freshwater, causing constant osmotic water influx that must be expelled.

options.text: Their internal environment is hypotonic relative to freshwater, so water constantly leaves
options.explanation: If the internal environment were hypotonic, water would leave and the amoeba would not need to pump water out.

options.text: Their internal environment is isotonic to freshwater so the vacuole is not actually needed
options.explanation: If conditions were isotonic, there would be no need for a contractile vacuole.

options.text: The contractile vacuole pumps water in to keep the cell from shrinking in freshwater
options.explanation: The vacuole pumps water out, not in; the amoeba is constantly gaining water by osmosis.

toLevel5.stem: A medical student suggests using distilled water to wash wounds because it is the purest option. Evaluate this suggestion.

options.text: Unwise; distilled water is hypotonic and could cause lysis of exposed cells at the wound
options.explanation: Distilled water would draw water into cells at the wound site, potentially damaging tissue by causing cell lysis.

options.text: Excellent advice; distilled water is the safest and most sterile option for wound care
options.explanation: While sterile, distilled water's hypotonic nature can damage cells; isotonic saline is preferred.

options.text: Unwise; but only because distilled water contains harmful chemicals from the distillation
options.explanation: The issue is osmotic damage to cells, not chemical contamination.

options.text: Excellent; all hospitals use distilled water exclusively for cleaning all wounds routinely
options.explanation: Hospitals typically use isotonic saline for wound irrigation to avoid osmotic damage.

toLevel5.stem: A researcher notices that red blood cells placed in a solution containing a cell-permeable solute do not change volume, even though the total solute concentration is higher outside. Why?

options.text: The permeable solute equilibrates across the membrane, so it does not affect tonicity
options.explanation: Only non-penetrating solutes affect tonicity; permeable solutes distribute equally across the membrane and do not drive net water movement.

options.text: The cells pumped out enough water to match the higher external concentration exactly
options.explanation: Red blood cells cannot actively pump water; the explanation relates to solute permeability.

options.text: The cell membrane became impermeable to water due to the permeable solute binding to it
options.explanation: The membrane remains permeable to water; the permeable solute equilibrates and does not create an osmotic gradient.

options.text: The experiment must have failed because higher external concentration always causes crenation
options.explanation: Only non-penetrating solutes cause crenation; permeable solutes do not create an effective osmotic gradient.

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that drinking too much water too quickly can be dangerous because it dilutes the blood. Evaluate this claim using osmotic principles.

options.text: Correct; excess water makes blood hypotonic, potentially causing cells to swell and lyse
options.explanation: Excessive water intake can dilute blood plasma, making it hypotonic relative to cells, which can cause dangerous swelling.

options.text: Incorrect; the body can always process any amount of water without osmotic consequences
options.explanation: The body has limits; rapid excess water intake can overwhelm osmoregulation and cause hyponatremia.

options.text: Correct; but only because water contains dissolved toxins that poison blood cells directly
options.explanation: The danger is osmotic dilution, not toxins in the water.

options.text: Incorrect; water is always beneficial and cannot cause any harm to cells in any quantity
options.explanation: Water intoxication is a real medical condition caused by osmotic imbalance.

toLevel5.stem: Some marine invertebrates are osmoconformers, meaning their internal solute concentration matches seawater. How does this strategy affect their cells?

options.text: Their cells experience no net water movement because they are isotonic to their environment
options.explanation: By matching internal solute concentration to seawater, there is no osmotic gradient and cells maintain normal volume.

options.text: Their cells constantly swell because seawater is always hypotonic to all living cells
options.explanation: Seawater is hypertonic to most land organisms but isotonic to osmoconformers by definition.

options.text: Their cells shrink because matching seawater concentration causes excessive water loss always
options.explanation: If concentrations match, there is no net water movement and cells do not shrink.

options.text: Their cells have no membranes so osmosis cannot occur regardless of the environment used
options.explanation: All cells have membranes; osmoconformers simply match their internal concentration to the environment.

toLevel5.stem: A pharmaceutical company tests a new drug dissolved in 3% NaCl for injection. A scientist objects. What is the most likely concern?

options.text: 3% NaCl is strongly hypertonic and would cause crenation of blood cells near the injection site
options.explanation: 3% NaCl far exceeds the isotonic 0.9%, creating a hypertonic environment that would damage cells.

options.text: 3% NaCl is too dilute and would cause haemolysis of red blood cells in the bloodstream
options.explanation: 3% NaCl is hypertonic, not hypotonic; it would cause crenation, not haemolysis.

options.text: NaCl is toxic to all cells at any concentration so it should never be used in injections
options.explanation: NaCl at 0.9% is safely used in IV solutions; the concern is specifically the hypertonic concentration.

options.text: The drug would not dissolve properly in 3% NaCl because the concentration is too high
options.explanation: The primary concern is osmotic damage to cells, not drug solubility.

toLevel5.stem: Freshwater amoebae use {{blank:1}} to expel excess water that enters by osmosis because their cytoplasm is {{blank:2}} to the surrounding freshwater.

options.text: contractile vacuoles
options.explanation: Contractile vacuoles actively pump out excess water to prevent the cell from swelling and bursting.

options.text: mitochondria
options.explanation: Mitochondria produce ATP; they do not pump water out of cells.

options.text: ribosomes
options.explanation: Ribosomes synthesise proteins; they are not involved in water regulation.

options.text: hypertonic
options.explanation: The amoeba's cytoplasm has a higher solute concentration than freshwater, drawing water in by osmosis.

options.text: hypotonic
options.explanation: If the cytoplasm were hypotonic, water would leave, not enter.

options.text: isotonic
options.explanation: If conditions were isotonic, no excess water would enter and no vacuole would be needed.

toLevel5.stem: Drinking excessive water can make blood plasma {{blank:1}} relative to blood cells, potentially causing {{blank:2}} of those cells.

options.text: hypotonic
options.explanation: Excess water dilutes blood plasma solutes, making it hypotonic relative to cells.

options.text: hypertonic
options.explanation: Adding water dilutes, not concentrates, the plasma.

options.text: isotonic
options.explanation: Excess water shifts the balance away from isotonic conditions.

options.text: swelling and lysis
options.explanation: Water enters cells from the hypotonic plasma, causing them to swell and potentially burst.

options.text: crenation only
options.explanation: Crenation occurs in hypertonic conditions; hypotonic conditions cause swelling.

options.text: rapid division
options.explanation: Osmotic stress does not cause cell division; it causes volume changes.
